title: Stop Touching Your Keyboard. Use This AI-Powered Microphone Instead
gist: London startup Relay, founded by two ex-Nothing employees, is building a dedicated $150 voice-to-text microphone (Relay Q, shipping early 2027) plus a Gemini-powered macOS agent app now in beta, competing against software-only dictation tools and rival wearable mics (Sandbar's Stream Ring, Pebble's Index 01) in an emerging AI-input-hardware category.

themes.theme: AI dictation hardware as a new category

insights.claim: Relay, a London startup founded by former Nothing employees Cookie Xu (ex-head of AI and services) and Raymond Zhu (hardware product manager), is building a dedicated portable microphone, the Relay Q, to deliver high-fidelity voice-to-text specifically because software-only tools fail at extreme speaking volumes in shared office settings.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: Signals a nascent wave of AI-native input peripherals (dedicated mics, rings) monetizing hardware plus subscription software, a potential new sub-category competing for share of the keyboard/smartphone input market.
insights.locator: Zhu's account of working at Nothing

insights.claim: The Relay Q hardware will cost $150, includes one year of Relay's software, and converts to a $15/month subscription afterward; the software itself can also be used standalone without buying the hardware.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: A hardware-plus-recurring-subscription model gives Relay a second monetization layer beyond the one-time device sale, a template other AI-hardware entrants may replicate.
insights.locator: pricing paragraph near end of article

insights.claim: Relay's software launches now for macOS only, with Windows, iOS, and Android planned later, while the Relay Q hardware itself will not ship until early 2027.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: A roughly year-long software-to-hardware launch gap lets Relay build a user base and gather usage data before committing to hardware manufacturing and inventory risk.

insights.claim: Relay deliberately rejected the smart-ring form factor used by rival voice-to-text wearables Sandbar's Stream Ring and Pebble's Index 01, reasoning that the ring category is already crowded, and instead built a handheld/clippable cylinder shape.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: Indicates the emerging whisper-to-text wearable niche is fragmenting into competing form factors before reaching mass adoption, worth tracking for which design converges as the standard.
insights.locator: paragraph on Sandbar's Stream Ring and Pebble's Index 01

themes.theme: Google's leverage as the underlying AI layer

insights.claim: Relay's voice-to-text engine is powered by Google's Gemini models rather than a proprietary model built by the startup itself.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: Even branded, funded AI hardware startups outside Google's ecosystem are choosing to build on Gemini rather than train their own models, reinforcing Google's position as a default infrastructure supplier across third-party AI products.
insights.locator: paragraph on hotkey setup and dictation engine

insights.claim: In hands-on testing, the author found Relay's Gemini-powered transcription noticeably less accurate than Google's own native Rambler dictation feature on the Pixel 11, suggesting first-party OS/hardware/model integration retains an accuracy edge over third-party apps built on the same underlying model.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: Implies model access alone (via API) doesn't close the gap with vertically integrated first-party products, a competitive moat consideration for platform owners like Google versus app-layer startups.
insights.locator: paragraph comparing Relay to Google's Rambler feature

insights.claim: Relay's app can execute contextual 'Skills' beyond dictation, such as opening Slack, finding a recipient, and drafting a message, or creating a Google Calendar event, moving the product up the stack from transcription to autonomous task execution.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: Voice-input products are converging with agentic automation, meaning competitive value is shifting from raw transcription accuracy toward reliable multi-app task execution.

insights.claim: Running Relay's Skills requires granting the app broad system permissions, including always-on microphone access and optional screen-snapshot capture, which the author explicitly compares to the privacy and security trade-offs raised by Microsoft's Recall feature.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: Broad OS-level permission requests for AI agents are a recurring flashpoint for consumer backlash and regulatory scrutiny (as seen with Microsoft Recall), a reputational risk any AI hardware/software vendor requesting similar access should be watched for.

insights.claim: Relay says it stores data locally on-device (user-editable/deletable) and that data passed to Relay's and then Google's servers for processing is not retained by Relay, an architecture that depends on trusting the vendor's non-retention claims.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: Unverifiable non-retention claims are a common but scrutiny-prone privacy posture in AI hardware products; investors evaluating such startups should weigh this as an unaudited assertion, not a guarantee.
insights.locator: paragraph on data storage and processing

insights.claim: In the author's beta testing, Relay's automation was inconsistent: it struggled to reliably trigger the Slack skill and inserted emoji unpredictably, while it reliably created a Google Calendar event and correctly supplied a Google Maps link during a message dictation.
insights.speaker: Julian Chokkattu
insights.so_what: Illustrates that agentic voice products remain unreliable at the beta stage, a maturity gap that will determine how quickly this category can win mainstream trust.
insights.locator: paragraphs describing emoji and Slack/Calendar skill tests
